title_and18_spoken_English_para_plan.spoken: On Friday 5 December 1952, cold, stagnant air descended on London.
Overhead, warmer air pressed down like a lid, holding the chill captive beneath.
Londoners were accustomed to murky, dreary winters.
This time, though, the capital's smoke was trapped too, thickening into a choking smog, a mix of smoke and fog.
That smoke, from coal burned in domestic fireplaces and power stations, was laden with soot and noxious sulphur dioxide.
In places, visibility fell to a few metres.
Ambulance services were suspended, an opera at the Sadler's Wells theatre was abandoned at the interval, and prize cattle at the Smithfield agricultural show died or had to be slaughtered.
The smog dissipated on Tuesday 9 December.
Officials at the time put the excess deaths at about 4,000, but a 1954 Ministry of Health report blamed later deaths on influenza.

A study published in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2001 reassessed the evidence and cast doubt on that explanation, estimating about 12,000 excess deaths between December 1952 and February 1953.
For decades Londoners had tolerated the smoke as a nuisance.
One villain flickered in their own grates, a source of warmth and comfort so habitual that few thought to accuse it.
Such complacency may help to explain the government's grudging response.
It withstood pressure for an inquiry until May 1953.
Reform proved protracted, slowed by official inertia.
The Clean Air Act became law on 5 July 1956, three and a half years after the smog.
It empowered municipal councils to create smokeless zones, combating smoke at its source.
The cosy hearth, beloved of British families, had, all along, been among the chief offenders.
